# Guide: LinkedIn personal branding for founders in India: the complete guide
URL: https://boldface.online/playbook/linkedin-personal-branding-for-founders-india/
Author: Koushik Agarwalla, Boldface

In India, LinkedIn has become the place where founders get checked out. Investors, enterprise buyers, senior candidates and journalists all look you up there first. This guide brings together everything we've learned running LinkedIn for 35+ founders and executives across India, Dubai and Abu Dhabi.

### Why it matters for Indian founders

India is one of LinkedIn's largest markets, with well over 100 million members, and most founders still don't use it well. That's the opportunity. A founder with a clear point of view and a steady presence stands out quickly, and the benefits reach every part of the business:

- Fundraising. Investors arrive at the meeting already knowing how you think.

- Sales. B2B buyers trust founders they've read for months.

- Hiring. Good people want to work for founders they respect.

- Partnerships and invitations. Speaking slots, podcasts and collaborations find you.

### Step 1: Positioning

Decide what you want to be known for, and by whom. Not your company's tagline: your point of view. A fintech founder might want to be known for a sharp take on credit for small businesses. A D2C founder might want to be known as the person who understands Tier 2 consumers better than anyone. Pick three or four topics you'll own.

### Step 2: Profile

Rebuild your profile around that position. Headline, About, Featured, experience and banner should all say the same thing. Our [section by section profile checklist](https://boldface.online/playbook/linkedin-profile-optimisation-checklist/) walks through it.

### Step 3: Posts

Two or three posts a week is plenty. The ones that work for founders tend to be:

- Decisions you made and why

- Mistakes and what they taught you

- What you see in your market that others miss

- Lessons from customers, told carefully

- Behind the scenes of building the company

Write the first line with care; it decides whether anyone reads the rest. Our guide to [writing hooks](https://boldface.online/playbook/how-to-write-a-linkedin-hook/) helps.

### Step 4: Newsletter

Once you're posting consistently, a newsletter gives your most engaged followers more depth and lands in their notifications and email. Read [how to start a LinkedIn newsletter people actually open](https://boldface.online/playbook/how-to-start-a-linkedin-newsletter/).

### Step 5: Networking

Content gets you seen. Networking gets you in the room. Build a list of the people who matter, comment on their posts with something useful, and connect with a short, personal note. Never automate it. Here's [how to network without being that person](https://boldface.online/playbook/linkedin-networking-without-spam/).

### Step 6: Collaborations

Borrow audiences: co-written posts with respected peers, podcast and LinkedIn Live guest spots, and events. It's the fastest way to reach people who don't know you yet.

### Step 7: Your company page and team

When the founder's presence is working, bring in the leadership team and give the company page more to say. Read [company page or personal profile](https://boldface.online/playbook/company-page-vs-personal-profile/) for how to split the effort.

### How long it takes

- Engagement and follower growth: four to six weeks

- Inbound conversations: usually three to six months

- Being known for something in your industry: six to twelve months

For reference, a fintech founder in Mumbai we worked with went from 400 to 12,000 followers in nine months. A D2C beauty founder in Bangalore reached 8,000 in six months.

### What to measure

Track inbound first: messages, introductions and opportunities that trace back to your presence. Then reach among the right people, whether people link your name to your topics, and who's new in your network. Follower counts come last.

### Doing it yourself vs getting help

If you write well and can protect a few hours a week, you can do all of this yourself. If you can't, [compare an agency, a freelancer and an in-house hire](https://boldface.online/playbook/linkedin-agency-vs-freelancer-vs-in-house/), or see [how we work with founders](https://boldface.online/for/founders/).


# Guide: How to write a hook that does not start with I
URL: https://boldface.online/playbook/how-to-write-a-linkedin-hook/
Author: Koushik Agarwalla, Boldface

The first line of your LinkedIn post is doing one job. Not informing. Not entertaining. Not showcasing your expertise. Its only job is to make the reader stop scrolling and read the next line.

Most people write hooks that start with "I". "I recently realized..." "I have been thinking about..." "I want to share something..." The problem is not grammatical. The problem is that starting with "I" puts the focus on you before the reader has any reason to care about you.

### What actually stops the scroll

The hooks that perform consistently well share one characteristic: they create an open loop in the reader's mind. They raise a question, introduce a contradiction or state something that requires resolution.

- A number that surprises. "We grew from 800 to 11,000 followers in 5 months. Here is what we changed."

- A contradiction. "The best LinkedIn post I ever wrote had zero likes in the first hour."

- A direct challenge. "Most founders are wasting their time on LinkedIn. Here is the specific mistake."

- A story with immediate stakes. "Last Tuesday, a VC I had never spoken to DMed me about our round."

### The rule

Write your first line. Then ask yourself: does this create a question the reader needs to answer? If the honest answer is no, rewrite it. The content can be brilliant. If the first line does not hook, nobody reads the brilliant content.

The best hooks are not clever. They are specific. Specificity creates curiosity. "I learned something about business" is ignored. "The conversation that changed how I price my work" gets clicks.

### A practical exercise

Write five first lines for your next post before you write anything else. Pick the one that makes you most want to know what comes next. That is your hook. The rest of the post is just honouring the promise you made in that first line.


# Guide: The 5 post types that actually generate inbound
URL: https://boldface.online/playbook/linkedin-post-types-that-generate-inbound/
Author: Koushik Agarwalla, Boldface

Most LinkedIn content gets likes. Some gets comments. Very little generates real business: DMs, meeting requests, partnership conversations, inbound leads. The difference is almost always the format.

After managing LinkedIn for 35+ founders and brands, we have seen exactly which post types move the needle on actual business outcomes versus vanity metrics. Here are the five that work.

### 1. The Contrarian Take

Pick a widely held belief in your industry and argue against it, with evidence. Not for the sake of being controversial, but because you genuinely believe the conventional wisdom is wrong. This is the single highest-performing post type for authority building. It positions you as someone who thinks independently and has the conviction to say so publicly.

### 2. The Behind-the-Scenes Number

Share a specific metric from your business or work with context. Not "we grew" but "we went from 12 inbound calls a month to 47 in 90 days by changing one thing in our LinkedIn profile." Numbers with context are credibility. They show you are someone who measures, which means you are someone who delivers.

### 3. The Lesson from a Failure

The most-shared posts on LinkedIn are almost never success stories. They are honest, specific accounts of something that went wrong and what the person learned. Vulnerability, when it is genuine and not performed, generates more trust than any highlight reel.

### 4. The Decision Framework

Walk your audience through how you make a specific type of decision. How do you evaluate a new hire? How do you decide which clients to take on? How do you think about pricing? Frameworks are shareable because they are useful, and useful content gets passed around.

### 5. The Direct Recommendation

Recommend a book, a tool, a person, a resource, with genuine specificity about why. "This book changed how I think about X" is weak. "Chapter 7 of this book gave me a framework I use every week in client conversations" is specific enough to be trusted. The person you recommend will often see it. New doors open.


# Guide: LinkedIn profile optimisation: a section by section checklist
URL: https://boldface.online/playbook/linkedin-profile-optimisation-checklist/
Author: Koushik Agarwalla, Boldface

Before almost every important meeting, the other person looks you up. Your LinkedIn profile does the selling before you've said a word. This checklist goes section by section. Work through it in order, because the early sections matter most.

### Before you start: positioning

Write one sentence: “I want to be known by [these people] for [this thing].” Every section below should support it. If you can't write the sentence, start there. Our guide to [why your LinkedIn bio is quietly killing your credibility](https://boldface.online/playbook/linkedin-headline-and-about-section/) helps.

### Photo

- Recent, well lit, your face filling most of the frame

- Looking at the camera, dressed the way you would for an important meeting

- Plain or softly blurred background

### Banner

- Reinforces your positioning: a line about what you do, your company, your newsletter or a talk

- Readable on a phone, where most people will see it

- Not a stock photo of a city skyline

### Headline

- Says what you do, who for and what changes for them

- Uses the words your audience would search for

- Skips the stack of titles: “CEO | Speaker | Mentor | Investor” tells nobody anything

### About

- The first two lines show before “see more”, so lead with the reader's problem or your point of view

- Written in the first person, the way you talk

- Includes proof: numbers, outcomes, notable work

- Ends with a clear next step: what to message you about, or where to find your newsletter

### Featured

- Three or four items a stranger should see first

- Your best post, a talk or podcast, your newsletter, a case study or your company

- Updated every few months

### Experience

- Outcomes, not duties: what changed because you were there

- Current role written with the most care

- Older roles kept short

### Skills, recommendations and the rest

- Top skills match your positioning, not everything you've ever done

- Two or three recent recommendations from people your audience respects

- A custom profile URL with your name

- Creator mode tools, if available to you, with topics that match your positioning

### The final test

Show your profile to someone who doesn't know you for ten seconds, then ask them what you do and who you do it for. If they can't answer, go back to the headline and About.

Want an outside eye? We do [LinkedIn profile audits](https://boldface.online/services/linkedin-audit/) with a ranked fix list, or [rebuild the whole profile](https://boldface.online/services/linkedin-profile-optimisation/) for you.


# Guide: Why your LinkedIn bio is quietly killing your credibility
URL: https://boldface.online/playbook/linkedin-headline-and-about-section/
Author: Koushik Agarwalla, Boldface

You have three seconds. That is the average time someone spends deciding whether to accept your connection request, click your profile or keep scrolling. In those three seconds, two things are doing all the work: your profile photo and your headline.

Most LinkedIn headlines read like a job title. "Founder at X" or "CEO | Helping companies grow" or the worst: "Entrepreneur | Speaker | Author | Consultant." None of these answer the only question the reader is actually asking: why should I care about you?

### What your headline is actually for

Your headline is not a job description. It is a value proposition. It should tell someone what you do, who you do it for and what outcome you create, in under twelve words. That is a hard constraint. It forces clarity.

Weak: "Founder & CEO | Passionate about startups"Strong: "I help D2C founders build LinkedIn audiences that convert to revenue"

### The About section nobody reads, and why

Most About sections are written in the third person or are structured like a CV. Neither of these work because LinkedIn is a conversational platform. The About section that performs is written like a direct message to your ideal reader. First person. Specific. Ending with a clear ask or invitation.

### The fix, in order

- Rewrite your headline as a value proposition. Who do you help, with what, to achieve what outcome.

- Rewrite your About section in first person, starting with the problem your ideal client has.

- Add a Featured section with your best content, a case study or a direct CTA.

- Make sure your banner image says something, not nothing.

These four changes take two hours. The compounding effect of getting them right lasts for years.


# Guide: How to start a LinkedIn newsletter people actually open
URL: https://boldface.online/playbook/how-to-start-a-linkedin-newsletter/
Author: Koushik Agarwalla, Boldface

A LinkedIn post has a short life. It shows up in the feed for a day or two, reaches whoever the algorithm picks, and then it's gone. A LinkedIn newsletter works differently. Every subscriber gets a notification and an email when a new issue goes out, and when you launch, LinkedIn invites your network to subscribe.

That makes it the closest thing LinkedIn has to an owned channel. It's also the most commonly abandoned one. Plenty of newsletters launch with a burst of subscribers and go quiet by issue four. Here's how to start one that doesn't.

### 1. Pick one promise, not a topic

“Thoughts on fintech” is a topic. “One lending decision a week, explained by someone who has signed off on thousands” is a promise. The promise tells people exactly what they get and why they should get it from you. Write yours in one sentence before you do anything else. If you can't, you're not ready to launch.

### 2. Name it so people remember it

The name shows up in notifications and inboxes, so it does real work. Short beats clever. A name that hints at the promise beats one that only makes sense to you. Avoid your own name plus “Insights”; nobody remembers those.

### 3. Choose a rhythm you can keep for a year

Weekly works if you have a lot to say and your industry moves fast. Fortnightly or monthly suits most founders and executives. The test is simple: could you keep this pace through your busiest quarter? A monthly newsletter that never misses beats a weekly one that disappears in March.

### 4. Write one idea per issue

Most good issues land somewhere between 600 and 1,200 words, and almost all of them make one point well. A useful structure:

- Open with a specific moment: a meeting, a number, a decision.

- Say what you think about it, plainly.

- Explain why, with the reasoning or evidence only you have.

- End with what the reader should do or watch for.

Resist the roundup format, five links with a line each, unless curation genuinely is your value. It's easy to write and easy to ignore.

### 5. Plan the first six issues before you launch

Launch week brings the most attention you'll get, so the first issue needs to be your strongest. Plan six issues up front. It proves the idea has legs and gives you a buffer for the weeks when work gets in the way.

### 6. Grow it on purpose

- Write a post for each issue that stands on its own and points to the full piece.

- Put the newsletter in your Featured section.

- Mention it in your headline or About if it's central to what you do.

- Share specific issues in conversations where they genuinely help.

- Keep growing your network with the right people. Subscribers come from your network first.

### 7. Personal profile or company page?

A newsletter from your personal profile builds trust in you. One from your company page builds the brand. If you're a founder starting from zero, start personal. People subscribe to people. You can always add a company newsletter later, once your [company page](https://boldface.online/services/linkedin-company-page-management/) has an audience of its own.

### The short version

One clear promise, a name people remember, a rhythm you can keep, one idea per issue, and six issues planned before launch. Do that and you'll be ahead of most newsletters on LinkedIn.

If you'd rather someone else ran it, [we manage LinkedIn newsletters end to end](https://boldface.online/services/linkedin-newsletter-management/): setup, calendar, every issue written in your voice, and growth.


# Guide: How to network on LinkedIn without being that person
URL: https://boldface.online/playbook/linkedin-networking-without-spam/
Author: Koushik Agarwalla, Boldface

You know the message. You accept a connection request and within a minute there's a pitch in your inbox. Three paragraphs about their services, a calendar link, and a follow-up two days later asking if you saw it.

Nobody wants to be that person, so most senior people swing the other way and don't network on LinkedIn at all. That's a mistake. Done properly, LinkedIn is the best networking tool there has ever been. Here's how to use it without becoming the person everyone mutes.

### 1. Start with a list, not a message

Write down the 50 to 100 people who would change your next year if they knew you. Investors you'd like to raise from. Buyers at companies you want as clients. Peers you respect. Organisers of events you'd like to speak at. People you'd like to hire.

This list is the whole strategy. Without it, networking turns into connecting with whoever shows up in your feed.

### 2. Be visible before you're in their inbox

Before you send anything, spend a few weeks being useful in public. Read what the people on your list post and leave comments that add something: a counterpoint, an example from your own work, a question that shows you actually read it. “Great post!” doesn't count.

Done consistently, this changes everything. When your connection request finally arrives, it's from someone they already recognise.

### 3. Write connection notes like a person

A good connection note is short and specific. It says why you're reaching out and asks for nothing.

Your post on credit underwriting for gig workers was the clearest thing I've read on it. We've been seeing the same pattern from the lender side. Would be good to be connected.

No pitch. No calendar link. No “I'd love to pick your brain”.

### 4. Let the relationship breathe

After connecting, keep doing what you were doing: commenting, sharing their work when it's genuinely good, replying to their stories. If there's a natural reason to talk, a funding round, a new role, a post where you have something real to add, send a short message. Ask for a conversation only once there's a reason for one.

### 5. Make the DM easy to say yes to

When you do ask, be specific about why and keep it small. “Would you be open to a 20 minute call next week? I'd like to compare notes on how you're handling enterprise procurement” gets far more yeses than “Let's connect sometime”.

### 6. Never automate it

Automation tools promise hundreds of connections a week. What they deliver is hundreds of strangers who've seen your name attached to a template. LinkedIn's user agreement doesn't allow most of these tools, and accounts that use them get restricted. Your reputation is worth more than the time saved.

### 7. Keep score of the right things

Connection counts don't matter. Track how many people on your list now know who you are, how many conversations you've had, and what came out of them. Ten real relationships a quarter is a very good result.

### Where content fits in

Networking and content feed each other. Your posts give people a reason to accept your request, and your network gives your posts the right first readers. That's why we run [strategic networking](https://boldface.online/services/linkedin-networking/) and [content](https://boldface.online/services/linkedin-ghostwriting/) under one plan for our clients.


# Guide: What a LinkedIn ghostwriter actually does, and how to work with one
URL: https://boldface.online/playbook/what-a-linkedin-ghostwriter-does/
Author: Koushik Agarwalla, Boldface

“Ghostwriter” makes it sound like someone sits in a room inventing opinions for you. A good LinkedIn ghostwriter does almost the opposite. The job is to get what's already in your head onto the page, sounding like you on a good day.

### What the job actually involves

- Positioning. Working out what you should be known for and who needs to hear it.

- Extraction. Pulling stories, opinions and lessons out of you through calls and voice notes.

- Writing. Turning that raw material into posts with strong first lines and a clear point.

- Editing for voice. Making sure every post sounds like you and not like a writer.

- Planning. A calendar that balances your topics and formats over the month.

- Learning. Watching what works, what doesn't, and adjusting.

The writing is maybe a third of the work. The rest is thinking and listening.

### How voice gets captured

Your voice is the sum of small things: how long your sentences run, which words you'd never use, how direct you are, whether you're funny. A good ghostwriter learns these from how you actually talk. That's why we start every engagement with a long intake call and ask for voice notes, and why the first few weeks involve more back and forth than later on.

### How much of your time it takes

Less than you'd think, once it's running. A typical rhythm:

- A monthly call of 30 to 45 minutes to talk through what's on your mind

- Voice notes when something happens that's worth a post

- Approving drafts, usually on your phone

Most of our clients spend under 30 minutes a week.

### Is it honest?

As long as the ideas, experiences and opinions are yours, yes. Leaders have always had help with speeches, books and op-eds. The line is crossed when a ghostwriter invents experiences or opinions you don't hold. A good one never will.

### How to get great results from a ghostwriter

- Be honest in the intake. The specific, slightly uncomfortable stories make the best posts.

- Send raw material. A two minute voice note after a frustrating meeting is gold.

- Give direct feedback. “I'd never say that” helps more than polite approval.

- Approve quickly. Timely posts go stale if they sit in your inbox for a week.

- Stay engaged with replies. Comments are where relationships start, so show up there yourself.

### What it shouldn't look like

Posts you don't recognise. Stories that never happened. A tone that changes every week. Engagement bait. If you see these, your ghostwriter is writing for the algorithm, not for you.

If you'd like to see how we approach it, here's our [LinkedIn ghostwriting service](https://boldface.online/services/linkedin-ghostwriting/).


# Guide: How to build a content strategy in 90 minutes
URL: https://boldface.online/playbook/linkedin-content-strategy-in-90-minutes/
Author: Koushik Agarwalla, Boldface

Most founders either have no content strategy, or an over-engineered one that collapses after two weeks. Neither works. What works is a simple, honest framework that takes 90 minutes to build and 20 minutes a week to maintain.

Here is the exact process we use with every new client.

### Minutes 0 to 20: Define the one person you are writing for

Not a demographic. A specific person. The CFO of a Series A startup who is skeptical of personal branding but curious. The D2C founder who is exhausted by ads and looking for an organic channel. Write their name down. Write what keeps them up at night. Everything else flows from this.

### Minutes 20 to 40: Pick three content pillars

Three topics you can write about indefinitely with genuine authority. Not broad topics like "leadership" or "growth" but specific angles. "What I have learned about pricing from working with 35 founders." "The mistakes early-stage D2C brands make on LinkedIn." "How I think about building in public." Three pillars, not more. Focus is the strategy.

### Minutes 40 to 60: Map your post formats

For each pillar, identify two post formats that feel natural to you. Some people write well in lists. Others write better in narrative form. Some founders are comfortable sharing numbers. Others prefer ideas and frameworks. The best content strategy is the one you can sustain, not the one that looks most impressive in a deck.

### Minutes 60 to 90: Build a 30-day calendar

Eight to ten posts in 30 days. Map them out. Do not write them yet; just assign a topic, a pillar and a format to each slot. This is your operating document. When you sit down to write, you are not staring at a blank page. You have a brief.

That is it. 90 minutes. The rest is execution, which is the hard part, and also the part we handle for you.


# Guide: What actually gets reach on LinkedIn in 2026
URL: https://boldface.online/playbook/what-gets-reach-on-linkedin/
Author: Koushik Agarwalla, Boldface

Every few months someone announces a new LinkedIn algorithm hack. Most of them are noise. LinkedIn changes the details often, and it doesn't publish exactly how the feed works. What follows isn't a secret formula. It's what we consistently see working across our clients' accounts, and what consistently doesn't.

### What helps

Real expertise, clearly shown. LinkedIn has said it wants to show people knowledge and advice from people who know what they're talking about. Posts that teach something specific, drawn from your own experience, tend to travel further and for longer than general commentary.

A consistent topic. When you post about the same few subjects, the people who care about them engage, and your posts find more people like them. Jumping between topics makes that harder.

Conversations in the comments. Thoughtful comments, and your replies to them, are a strong sign that a post is worth showing to more people. Reply to the good ones properly, especially in the first hour or two.

Posts people stop and read. A strong first line and a post worth finishing matter more than any trick. If people scroll past, nothing else helps.

Native formats. Document posts and carousels, short video and well formatted text all work when the content is good. Pick the format that suits the idea, not the one someone told you is favoured this month.

### What hurts

- Engagement bait. “Comment YES if you agree” posts and engagement pods tend to backfire, and LinkedIn has said it demotes them.

- Posting and disappearing. Ignoring the comments on your own post wastes its best moment.

- Too many outside links. In our experience, posts that send people off LinkedIn often travel less far. If a link matters, make the post useful on its own.

- Inconsistency. Three weeks of daily posts and then silence resets the progress you made.

- Automation. Mass connection requests and automated comments put your account at risk.

### How often to post

Two or three strong posts a week beats seven weak ones for most founders and executives. Quality and consistency matter more than volume. That's why we usually plan 8 to 12 posts a month for clients.

### What reach is actually for

Reach is a means, not the goal. A post seen by 2,000 of the right people beats one seen by 200,000 of the wrong ones. Measure who's engaging and what conversations follow, not only how many impressions you got. Our guide to [the five post types that actually generate inbound](https://boldface.online/playbook/linkedin-post-types-that-generate-inbound/) goes deeper.

If you'd like this handled for you, see our [LinkedIn content service](https://boldface.online/services/linkedin-ghostwriting/).


# Guide: The comment that got me three clients in one week
URL: https://boldface.online/playbook/linkedin-commenting-strategy/
Author: Koushik Agarwalla, Boldface

In January, I left a comment on a post by a founder I had never spoken to. It was 47 words. Within 72 hours, three people who had seen that comment had sent me a connection request. One of them became a client within the week.

I have since run this as a deliberate strategy for clients and the results are consistent. Strategic commenting is the most underused growth lever on LinkedIn. Here is why it works and exactly how to do it.

### Why comments outperform posts for reach

When you post original content, it reaches your existing network first. LinkedIn's algorithm decides how far it travels from there. When you comment on someone else's post, particularly one that is already performing well, your comment is seen by everyone who engages with that post. Many of them are not in your network. You are borrowing distribution from someone who has already earned it.

### The anatomy of a comment that works

A comment that builds your reputation does three things. It adds something the post did not already say. It demonstrates your specific expertise or perspective. And it makes the reader want to see more of what you think.

- Do not just agree. "Great post!" is noise. "This point about X resonates. We saw the same pattern when Y happened" is a contribution.

- Be specific. The more specific your observation, the more credible you appear.

- End with a question or a perspective that invites response. Conversations on LinkedIn are visible to everyone.

### The practical system

Identify 10 to 15 accounts your ideal clients follow. Check their posts every morning. Leave two to three substantive comments. Do this for 30 days. The compounding effect on your visibility and the quality of your inbound is significant. It takes 20 minutes a day. Most people do not do it because it feels small. That is exactly why it works.


# Guide: Company page or personal profile: where should founders post?
URL: https://boldface.online/playbook/company-page-vs-personal-profile/
Author: Koushik Agarwalla, Boldface

Almost every founder asks this question at some point. You have a company to build and limited time. Should your LinkedIn effort go into the company page or your personal profile?

The short answer: mostly your personal profile, with the company page doing a different job alongside it. Here's why, and how to split the work.

### People follow people

On LinkedIn, people engage with people far more than with logos. A post from a founder about a hard decision they made will almost always travel further than the same story posted by the company page. It feels like a conversation, not an announcement.

That's why, at the early stage especially, the founder's profile is often the company's most effective marketing channel. Investors, candidates and buyers all look up the founder.

### What the company page is for

The company page still matters. It just does a different job:

- Proof. It's where people check that you're real: size, team, what you do, how active you are.

- Official news. Launches, funding, partnerships, awards.

- Hiring. Jobs, culture and the people candidates would work with.

- Customer stories. Case studies and results, told carefully.

Think of the page as the shop window and the founder's profile as the person on the shop floor who actually talks to you.

### How to split your effort

For most early stage founders, something like 80 percent of the effort on the personal profile and 20 percent on the page is a sensible start. As the company grows, shift the balance: add the leadership team, and give the page more to say with customer stories, hiring and launches.

### Make them work together

- When the page announces something, the founder adds a personal take on why it matters.

- When the founder posts something that does well, the page can reshare it with context.

- Leadership team members post from their own expertise, so the company looks like a team, not one person.

- Employees get easy, optional prompts to share in their own words.

### When the company page should lead

There are exceptions. Large companies with many leaders, regulated businesses where individuals can't say much, and consumer brands where the product is the story may lean more on the page. Even then, the posts that do best tend to have a person in them.

### The bottom line

Founders: start with your own profile. Get it [positioned properly](https://boldface.online/services/linkedin-profile-optimisation/), post consistently, and let the company page carry the proof. When you're ready to bring in the leadership team and the page, that's what our [company page and teams](https://boldface.online/services/linkedin-company-page-management/) service is for.


# Guide: The C-suite guide to LinkedIn
URL: https://boldface.online/playbook/linkedin-for-c-suite-executives/
Author: Koushik Agarwalla, Boldface

If you are a CEO, CFO or CTO who has not posted on LinkedIn in the last six months, this is for you. Not a lecture about being "more active on social media." A practical case for why your absence is costing you things you care about.

The argument usually goes something like this: "I have a business to run. I close deals at dinners and on the phone. LinkedIn is for people who do not have real relationships." It is a reasonable position. It is also increasingly wrong.

### What happens before the dinner

Before a potential investor, client or board member agrees to a meeting, they do one thing: they search for you online. If they find a LinkedIn profile with a job title, a list of companies and no voice, they form an impression. That impression is of someone who is either not confident enough to say anything publicly or does not have anything interesting to say.

Neither is a great way to start a relationship. The dinner you are relying on never happens if the search does not go well first.

### The specific opportunity most C-suite leaders are missing

There is a category of opportunity that almost only comes through a visible personal brand: inbound from people who were not already in your network. Investor conversations initiated by someone who read your thinking about capital allocation. Board opportunities from a chairman who saw your post about governance. Talent reaching out because they want to work for someone who thinks the way you do.

These do not happen through your existing relationships. They happen through your public voice, or they do not happen at all.

### What "being on LinkedIn" actually requires

For a CFO or CTO, we are not talking about posting every day. We are talking about eight to ten posts a month, written in your voice, about things you genuinely think about. The financial strategy decisions you are wrestling with. The technology choices that actually matter. The leadership lessons you have earned.

You do not need to become an influencer. You need to be findable, legible and credible to the right people. That is a 20-minute-a-week commitment if you work with someone who knows what they are doing. The question is not whether you have time for LinkedIn. The question is whether you can afford to remain invisible to the people who are looking for someone exactly like you.


# Guide: The personal brand toolkit every CFO should have
URL: https://boldface.online/playbook/linkedin-personal-brand-for-cfos/
Author: Koushik Agarwalla, Boldface

Of all the C-suite roles, the CFO has perhaps the most underutilised personal brand potential. The CEO gets the profile pieces. The CTO gets the tech media coverage. The CFO, who arguably has the clearest, most credible view of how a business actually works, is almost always invisible online.

This is a significant missed opportunity. Not just for the individual CFO, but for the companies they work for and the candidates and investors they are trying to attract.

### Why CFO visibility matters more than you think

A CFO who writes publicly about financial strategy, capital allocation, the realities of fundraising or how to build a resilient P&L is signalling something that no press release can replicate: that this is a company run by adults who understand the fundamentals. Investors read CFO content differently from CEO content. They are looking for rigour, realism and the kind of unsentimental thinking that protects capital.

Beyond investor relations, a visible CFO attracts three things consistently: board advisory opportunities, executive recruiter attention and the interest of high-quality finance talent who want to work for someone they can learn from.

### What CFO content actually looks like

The mistake most CFOs make when they do try to post is writing about things that are too broad. Leadership lessons, general business advice, motivational observations. None of this is distinctive. What is distinctive is the specific, hard-won knowledge of someone who has lived inside the numbers of a real business.

- The financing decision you made and why, including what you ruled out and why.

- How you think about unit economics at different stages of growth.

- The one metric you watch more closely than any other and what it is telling you right now.

- What you wish founders understood about investor expectations before they walked into a Series A.

### The baseline toolkit

Every CFO who wants to build a credible digital presence needs exactly four things: a LinkedIn headline that describes what you do and who you do it for, an About section written in first person that starts with a problem your ideal reader has, a clear Featured section pointing to your best thinking, and a posting cadence of at least twice a month. That is the minimum. It is also, for most CFOs, more than their entire peer group is doing.

The bar is low. The opportunity is large. The question is simply whether you want to be the finance leader in your space who has a voice, or the one who does not.


# Guide: LinkedIn agency, freelancer or in-house: which should you hire?
URL: https://boldface.online/playbook/linkedin-agency-vs-freelancer-vs-in-house/
Author: Koushik Agarwalla, Boldface

Once you decide you need help with LinkedIn, there are three real options: a freelancer, an agency, or someone in-house. We run an agency, so we obviously have a side. But each option suits different people, and picking the wrong one wastes months. Here's an honest comparison.

### A freelance ghostwriter

Good for: one person who mainly needs posts written, and who's happy to steer the strategy themselves.

- Usually the most affordable option.

- You work directly with the writer, so the voice can get very close.

- Quality varies hugely. The best freelancers are excellent and booked up.

- Most freelancers write. Fewer handle positioning, networking, newsletters or a company page.

- If they get ill, busy or move on, your posting stops.

### An in-house hire

Good for: larger companies with several leaders and a company page that all need consistent attention.

- Full-time attention and deep knowledge of the business.

- The most expensive option once you count salary, management and tools.

- Hard to find one person who can do strategy, sharp writing, design, video and networking.

- Often pulled into other marketing work, so LinkedIn slips.

### A LinkedIn agency

Good for: founders and executives who want the whole thing handled, from positioning to posts to the people they need to know.

- Strategy, writing, design, newsletters, networking and the company page under one plan.

- Continuity: the work doesn't stop when one person is away.

- Costs more than a freelancer and less than a senior hire.

- The big risk: at many agencies a senior person sells the work and a junior person does it. Ask who will actually write your posts.

### Five questions that decide it

- Do you need strategy, or just writing? If you know exactly what you want to say, a good freelancer might be enough.

- How many people need to post? One person suits a freelancer or agency. A whole leadership team plus a page starts to justify an agency or in-house team.

- Do you need networking and collaborations too? Most freelancers don't do this.

- How much of your time can you give? The less time you have, the more strategy and initiative you need from whoever you hire.

- What happens if they leave? Ask about continuity before you sign.

### Our honest take

If you're a founder or executive who wants LinkedIn to bring in real opportunities and you don't have time to run it, an agency where senior people do the work is usually the best value. If you just need a few posts tidied up, hire a good freelancer. If you're a large company with ten leaders, build a small in-house team and bring in specialists where needed.

Whichever you choose, read [the ten questions to ask before you hire a LinkedIn agency](https://boldface.online/playbook/how-to-choose-a-linkedin-agency-india/) first. And if you want to see how we do it, here's [everything we handle](https://boldface.online/services/).


# Guide: How to choose a LinkedIn agency in India: 10 questions to ask first
URL: https://boldface.online/playbook/how-to-choose-a-linkedin-agency-india/
Author: Koushik Agarwalla, Boldface

Search for a LinkedIn agency in India and you'll find dozens that promise the same thing: thought leadership, growth, authority. The websites blur together. The difference shows up three months in, when you either have a voice people recognise or a feed full of posts that sound like everyone else's.

These are the ten questions we'd ask if we were hiring an agency ourselves. A good agency will answer every one of them without flinching.

### 1. Who will actually write my posts?

The most important question. At many agencies a senior person sells the work and a junior writer does it. Ask for the name of the person who'll write for you, and ask to talk to them before you sign.

### 2. How will you capture my voice?

Look for a real process: a long intake call, voice notes, a read through things you've written or said. If the answer is “we'll send you a questionnaire”, expect generic content.

### 3. Do you use automation for outreach or engagement?

Automated connection requests, comment pods and engagement groups can get accounts restricted and make you look like a spammer. The right answer is a flat no.

### 4. What happens before the first post?

A good agency starts with positioning: what you want to be known for and who you want to reach. If they want to start posting in week one without that, they're selling volume, not strategy.

### 5. Do I approve everything?

Nothing should go out under your name without your sign-off. Ask how approvals work and how long they take you each week.

### 6. What do you do beyond writing posts?

Posts are one part of LinkedIn. Ask whether they handle your profile, a newsletter, networking with the people who matter, collaborations and your company page, or whether you'll need other people for those.

### 7. What will you report on?

Followers and impressions are easy to report and easy to inflate. Ask whether they track inbound: the messages, introductions and opportunities that came from your presence. That's the number that matters.

### 8. Can I see real case studies?

Ask for specific before and after examples with numbers and timeframes. Names may be confidential, but the details shouldn't be vague.

### 9. What's the notice period?

Long lock-ins are a warning sign. A confident agency works month to month with a reasonable notice period, because it expects you to stay for the results.

### 10. Will you tell me if we're not a fit?

Good agencies turn work down. If they'll take anyone who can pay, they won't be selective about the quality of your work either.

### Red flags

- Guaranteed follower numbers or “viral” posts

- Packages priced by number of posts with no mention of strategy

- Samples that all sound the same, whoever they were written for

- Any mention of pods, automation or growth hacks

- Pressure to sign a six or twelve month contract up front

For what it's worth, here's how we answer these: Koushik plans, writes and runs every engagement, we never use automation, everything is approved by you, and it's a monthly retainer with 30 days' notice. Read the [case studies](https://boldface.online/work/) and decide for yourself, or compare the options in [agency vs freelancer vs in-house](https://boldface.online/playbook/linkedin-agency-vs-freelancer-vs-in-house/).


# Guide: How to write about failure on LinkedIn without it backfiring
URL: https://boldface.online/playbook/writing-about-failure-on-linkedin/
Author: Koushik Agarwalla, Boldface

The most-shared, most-commented, most-DM-generating posts on LinkedIn are almost never about success. They are about failure. A deal that fell apart. A hire that went wrong. A strategy that made perfect sense and produced the opposite of the intended result.

This is not an accident. Failure posts work because they are rare. Most of what gets published on LinkedIn is sanitised, polished and optimistic. When someone tells the truth about something that went wrong, it stands out immediately. The contrast alone creates engagement.

### Why most failure posts backfire

The problem is that most people write failure posts incorrectly. They make one of two mistakes. The first is being vague: "I made some mistakes early in my career. Here is what I learned." This sounds like wisdom but feels like nothing. There is no story, no stakes, no specificity. Nobody is moved by a lesson without a scene.

The second mistake is over-performing vulnerability. The post that is clearly designed to seem humble rather than actually be humble. Readers can feel this immediately, and the trust damage is worse than saying nothing at all. Performed vulnerability is the most corrosive content you can publish.

### The structure that works

A failure post that builds your credibility instead of damaging it has four parts, in this order:

- The specific thing that went wrong, with enough detail that the reader can picture it.

- Why you made the decision you made, the logic that seemed reasonable at the time.

- What actually happened and what it cost you.

- The one thing you now do differently as a direct result.

Notice what is not on that list: a redemption arc that makes you look better than when you started, a list of generic lessons that could apply to anyone, or a tone that suggests you have fully resolved and transcended the failure.

### The test

Before you post it, ask one question: does this make me slightly uncomfortable? Not because it is unprofessional, but because it is honest. If the answer is no, if the post feels completely safe to publish, it is probably not specific or vulnerable enough to work. The posts that perform best are the ones where the author thought twice before hitting publish. That hesitation is the signal that you are saying something real.


# Guide: Why consistency beats brilliance on LinkedIn every single time
URL: https://boldface.online/playbook/linkedin-consistency/
Author: Koushik Agarwalla, Boldface

Every founder we have worked with has, at some point, published what they believed was their best post. The one they spent the most time on. The one with the sharpest insight, the cleanest structure, the most carefully chosen words. And sometimes it performed well. But more often than not, it was outperformed within the same month by something they wrote in 15 minutes on a Wednesday morning.

This is not a coincidence. It is a pattern. And it has taught us something important about how LinkedIn actually works: the algorithm rewards regularity more than it rewards quality. But more importantly, so do people.

### How trust is actually built online

Think about the last time you reached out to someone you had been following on LinkedIn. The reason you reached out was not because of one post. It was because of ten posts, or twenty, spread over several months, that consistently made you think a specific thing about that person: that they understand this topic, that they think clearly, that they are worth talking to.

That accumulation of small impressions is how trust is built. No single post creates it. Consistency is the mechanism. Quality is the content of each individual moment.

### What consistency actually requires

When most people think about consistency, they imagine an exhausting daily posting schedule that requires them to manufacture opinions they do not have. This is not what we mean. For the founders and executives we work with, consistency means eight to ten posts a month, roughly twice a week, each one specific, honest and worth reading.

That is achievable. It is also, for almost anyone we have worked with, more than they were doing before. The gap between where most leaders are and where they need to be is not a gap of brilliance. It is a gap of regularity.

### The practical implication

If you are choosing between writing one exceptional post a month and two decent posts a week, choose the two decent posts every time. The exceptional post will be forgotten. The two decent posts, repeated across six months, will build something that cannot be undone: a reputation for showing up.

Showing up is the strategy. Everything else is tactics.
